title: Evaluating a Deterministic Validator Plus Single‑Iteration Repair Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks; preregistration id cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) to test whether a minimal guarded pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation (declared model: gpt-5-mini) followed by a frozen deterministic configuration validator and at most one automated repair iteration—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration versus plain single‑shot generation. Execution completed 600 episodes and used 301 model calls. Observed outcomes: baseline = 299/300 valid (99.667%); guarded = 300/300 valid (100.0%); paired counts n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The single permitted automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). The preregistered planning assumption (baseline pass rate = 0.40) was contradicted by the observed near‑ceiling baseline, removing statistical headroom for the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction target. We report preregistered design choices, execution accounting, confirmatory statistics, a compact post‑hoc sensitivity bound tied to the archived contingency counts, and artifact‑grounded recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations. All run artifacts and analysis outputs are archived in the execution manifest and analysis artifact bundle referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction: Automating the translation of operator intent into device configuration promises faster NetOps workflows but raises operational risk when generated changes are misordered, incomplete, or unsafe. Prior surveys and system papers recommend pairing probabilistic generators (LLMs) with deterministic validators or simulators as floor‑safety nets, and propose generate→verify→repair architectures for agentic NetOps. Yet there are few preregistered, paired A/B experiments that quantify how a bounded guarded pipeline affects first‑pass misconfiguration rates under controlled sampling semantics. This study implements a narrowly scoped, preregistered paired experiment that evaluates a minimal guarded pipeline: a single shared LLM candidate per task (single‑shot generation), a frozen deterministic validator performing rule and dependency checks, and at most one automated repair attempt when the validator detects violations. Research question: Can this minimal guarded pipeline reduce first‑pass misconfiguration relative to plain single‑shot generation under a controlled paired design? Contributions: (1) a preregistered confirmatory paired experiment with deterministic seed generation and archival of model outputs, validator traces, and repair traces; (2) artifact‑grounded confirmatory statistics showing a near‑ceiling baseline and a single corrected discordance; (3) a concise post‑hoc sensitivity quantification grounded in the archived contingency counts; (4) concrete operational recommendations and threats‑to‑validity grounded in the archived run.
sections.related_work: Empirical and survey literature shows LLMs can synthesize configuration templates or translate high‑level intent into device commands in controlled or lab settings, while also documenting systematic failure modes—hallucination, misordering, and overconfidence—that threaten operational safety. Cross‑domain evidence (medical QA, code generation) demonstrates that retrieval augmentation, deterministic verifiers, and bounded repair loops reduce factual errors and improve grounding; NetOps architecture proposals commonly recommend deterministic validators as floor‑safety nets. However, existing NetOps demonstrations are typically small‑scale or descriptive; reproducible, preregistered paired experiments that fix sampling semantics, use frozen validators, and bound automated repair budgets are rare. Our experiment situates itself at this intersection by providing a preregistered paired test with full artifact archival and deterministic task generation.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory hypotheses: The experiment was preregistered (id cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) and frozen before execution. The preregistration explicitly used a planning baseline pass‑rate assumption of 0.40 (this numeric assumption was used for power planning and is reported in the preregistration record archived with the run; the preregistration SHA is recorded in the execution manifest). Confirmatory hypotheses: H1 — the guarded pipeline reduces first‑pass misconfiguration rate by ≥50% (relative) versus single‑shot generation; H2 — one or fewer automated repair iterations recover ≥75% of initially invalid configurations.

Design and sampling semantics: A paired within‑task design was used with 300 deterministically generated seeds from the frozen task generator (planned episodes = 600). For each seed the same sampled LLM candidate was shared between both arms (shared_initial_candidate semantics): baseline (single‑shot generation) and guarded (same candidate validated and—if invalid—subjected to up to one automated repair attempt). The preregistered decision to reuse the initial candidate per pair increases within‑pair correlation and reduces the count of informative discordant pairs available to McNemar inference; this choice was preserved from the preregistration and is disclosed here as a material design factor affecting inferential power.

Model, validator, and scoring: The declared model in the execution contract was gpt-5-mini. The frozen deterministic validator/repair adapter (validator id deterministic_netops_validator_v5) performs rule‑ and dependency‑based checks, canonicalizes configurations to normalized command sequences/ASTs, and emits binary pass/fail scoring together with violation codes used to trigger automated repair. Scoring semantics implement full intent‑constraint validation: an output is scored as success only when the validator deems required command sequences and dependency constraints satisfied. The experiment treated model/provider failures according to the preregistered missingness plan (one retry allowed); the primary analysis treatment ('complete_pair_primary') drops pairs only if both calls fail.

Primary estimand and analysis plan: The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistered primary test is the exact McNemar two‑sided test (α=0.05) on paired pass/fail outcomes. We report the absolute risk difference with a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, bootstrap seed fixed) as prespecified. Secondary analyses include repair success rate with exact binomial intervals and sensitivity checks for missingness and contamination. All per‑task artifacts, validator traces, and analysis code were archived as part of the execution manifest and analysis artifact bundle.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and manifest summary: Planned episodes = 600, completed episodes = 600, complete pairs = 300, model_calls_used = 301; the repair stage invoked its single allowed model call exactly once under the preregistered repair budget. No provider or infrastructure failures occurred under the retry policy; all episodes were scorable under the preregistered rules.

Primary outcomes (artifact‑derived): Baseline_success_count = 299/300 (99.667%); Guarded_success_count = 300/300 (100.0%). Paired contingency counts (artifact summary): n11 = 299 (both success), n10 = 1 (guarded success, baseline fail), n01 = 0 (guarded fail, baseline success), n00 = 0 (both fail). These counts derive directly from the archived contingency summary used for the confirmatory inference.

Statistical inference (preregistered analyses): Exact McNemar two‑sided test on the observed contingency yields p = 1.00. Observed absolute paired difference (guarded minus baseline) = 1/300 ≈ 0.0033333. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the absolute paired difference = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples; archived bootstrap seed = 1729). Repair outcomes (H2): the single allowed automated repair corrected the sole initially invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1); exact Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0].

Post‑hoc sensitivity and inferential bound: The total observed discordant pairs (n10 + n01 = 1) sets a hard resolution limit on the run's resolvable absolute paired difference equal to 1/300 ≈ 0.00333 (the observed point estimate). With only one discordant pair the two‑sided exact McNemar calculation yields p = 1.00 because the test is driven by discordant counts; a single discordance supplies insufficient evidence to reject the null of no paired difference for the preregistered α. The paired bootstrap CI upper bound (0.01) bounds plausible absolute improvement under the run's sampling semantics. Because the preregistered power plan assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40, the observed near‑ceiling baseline invalidates that planning assumption and removes headroom for the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction target. This sensitivity statement and the numeric bounds are computed from the archived contingency summary and bootstrap outputs.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and operational implications: The guarded pipeline corrected the single invalid baseline output observed in this run, demonstrating that a frozen deterministic validator plus a bounded automated repair iteration can remediate validator‑detected violations in at least some cases. However, because the empirical baseline pass rate was far higher than the preregistered planning assumption, the experiment does not provide confirmatory evidence for the preregistered large relative effect (≥50%). The artifacted contingency counts and bootstrap CI quantify this limitation precisely.

Practical lessons for future confirmatory NetOps evaluations: (1) Calibrate task difficulty to produce a nontrivial baseline failure prevalence when the objective is to detect population‑level reductions in misconfiguration; preregister not only N but also target initial‑failure counts so power calculations map directly to expected discordant pairs in paired designs. (2) Pairing semantics materially affect detectability: sharing an initial candidate per pair increases within‑pair correlation and reduces discordant pairs for a given N; independent draws increase discordance potential but introduce cross‑arm heterogeneity—both choices should be preregistered and justified relative to the operational claim. (3) Repair budgets and human‑in‑the‑loop allowances should reflect the operational scenario under test; a single automated repair iteration is a conservative bound and may underrepresent production guardrail behavior.

Threats to validity: Internal validity is affected by the preregistered shared_initial_candidate decision (increasing within‑pair correlation). Construct validity is limited because the deterministic validator evaluates canonicalized configurations and constraint satisfaction rather than executing configurations in a live network; runtime packet‑level reachability, control‑plane effects, or performance consequences were not measured. External validity is limited by the synthetic task bank, constrained vendor‑template transformation set, a single model family (gpt-5-mini), and one validator implementation. Conclusion validity is constrained by the small number of informative discordant pairs; statistical inference about large preregistered effects is therefore unsupported by the observed data.

Reproducibility and artifact availability: All execution and analysis artifacts (raw model responses, per‑task normalized configurations, validator decisions, repair traces, contingency tables, bootstrap resamples, and analysis code) are archived in the run's execution manifest and analysis artifact bundle; readers may consult the archived manifest for exact artifact names and to reproduce the reported counts and intervals. The preregistration record and planning assumptions (including the numeric baseline assumption = 0.40) are archived with the run and referenced in the Disclosure Statement.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired experiment (N=300 pairs) using a frozen deterministic validator and a one‑iteration automated repair budget applied to gpt‑5‑mini outputs, baseline single‑shot generation was near‑ceiling (299/300) and the guarded pipeline produced 300/300 valid outputs. The single automated repair corrected the only observed invalid baseline output, but the run does not support the preregistered claim of ≥50% relative reduction in misconfiguration because the observed baseline contradicted the planning assumption (baseline pass rate = 0.40) and left no statistical headroom. Future confirmatory NetOps evaluations should calibrate task difficulty to produce sufficient initial failures, preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets explicitly, and measure runtime semantic effects via emulation when operational claims require them. The archived execution manifest and analysis artifacts enumerate all per‑task traces and the analysis outputs used to produce the reported statistics.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and constrained vendor‑template scope limit external validity to broad production environments.
Single LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a single validator implementation restrict generality across model families and validator designs.

The preregistered power plan assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40; the observed baseline (299/300) contradicted that assumption and removed headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction.
Sampling semantics (shared_initial_candidate) reused the same initial candidate across paired arms, increasing within‑pair correlation and reducing discordant pairs available to McNemar inference.

Validation used deterministic configuration/constraint checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantic effects; actual runtime consequences of configurations were not executed and remain unmeasured.

H2 repair‑success evidence is based on a single initially invalid case (1/1 → 100%), yielding a wide Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]; larger counts of initial failures are required to estimate repair effectiveness precisely.
